topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - nature.com
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European public health contexts; findings may not directly transfer to private sector AI literacy programs or non-European healthcare systems, though competency frameworks have conceptual transferability.
takeaways: Use this framework as a template to audit existing AI literacy programs in your organisation — identify which digital health competencies are being developed and which gaps need addressing.

The European focus means the regulatory context (GDPR, EU AI Act) differs from Australia; adapt competency criteria to align with local privacy laws and Australian healthcare standards when implementing locally.

Competency frameworks for digital public health can inform broader AI capability-building programs by clarifying which technical, ethical, and organisational skills matter most — consider mapping these to your staff's current levels.

articles.title: Mind the gap: an evidence gap analysis of digital literacy within public health systems in the European Union using two different frameworks - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Mind the gap: an evidence gap analysis of digital literacy within public health systems in the European Union using two different frameworks  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses specifically on digital literacy in public health systems across EU member states; findings may not generalise to private health sectors, non-EU countries, or non-health organisational contexts.
takeaways: Use evidence gap analysis frameworks to identify where digital literacy interventions are most needed within your organisation's operations — this structured approach reveals which roles or departments lack adequate training coverage.

Digital literacy in public health systems faces distinct challenges compared to other sectors; if you work in healthcare or similar regulated environments, benchmark your AI literacy programmes against health-sector-specific gaps rather than generic corporate models.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG perspective based on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, though findings reflect client base skew toward large enterprises and may not represent SMEs or public sector organisations equally.
takeaways: AI adoption requires deliberate workforce upskilling and reskilling programs aligned with your organisation's AI strategy — not just technology implementation — to realise capability gains and manage workforce transitions.

Identify which roles will be augmented by AI tools versus displaced, then design targeted learning pathways that help existing employees build AI literacy relevant to their specific job functions rather than generic AI training.
Establish clear communication about how AI changes employee roles and career progression; this transparency reduces anxiety and improves engagement with AI capability-building initiatives.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - nature.com
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on middle school education contexts. Geographic scope and whether findings apply internationally or to other education levels unclear from snippet.
takeaways: AI literacy should be integrated as part of a broader digital literacy framework rather than taught in isolation, helping students understand AI's role within wider technological competencies.
Middle school is a critical intervention point for developing foundational AI understanding before students reach secondary education and workforce entry.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on faculty development in public health education, primarily higher education context. Generalisability to other sectors or non-academic settings unclear without full article details.
takeaways: Design faculty development programs that explicitly address and transform resistance to AI adoption, positioning readiness-building as a prerequisite for teaching AI literacy to students.

Use structured faculty development as a lever for organizational AI capability — upskilling educators first cascades AI understanding through their students and influences institutional culture around AI adoption.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited to higher education context. The four-domain model is conceptual and would need empirical validation across different institutional types and geographic regions to assess broader applicability.
takeaways: Consider framing AI literacy as a 'meta-skill' that integrates technical, critical thinking, ethical, and organisational domains — this broader framing helps employees see AI capability development as foundational rather than isolated technical training.

The four-domain model provides a framework for auditing your AI literacy programme: map which domains you're currently emphasising and identify gaps (e.g., are you covering ethical reasoning and change management alongside technical skills?).

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study design and sample characteristics not fully evident from the title and snippet alone. The framework appears conceptually applicable across sectors, but empirical scope (geography, industry, sample size) cannot be assessed from the information provided.
takeaways: AI-enabled work systems create dual pathways affecting wellbeing — some create strain (e.g. reduced autonomy, increased monitoring) while others provide resources (e.g. reduced cognitive load, skill development). Managers should actively design implementation to maximize resources and minimize strain.

Wellbeing outcomes depend not on AI adoption alone but on how work is restructured around it. Assess your current systems for both negative strain triggers and positive resource opportunities to identify intervention points.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - nature.com
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Findings are specific to nursing contexts and may not generalise to other professions or sectors. The three-wave design strengthens causal inference, but geographic scope and sample characteristics are unclear from the snippet alone.
takeaways: Preserving or expanding work autonomy is critical when implementing medical AI — nurses' wellbeing depends not just on AI readiness, but on retaining control over how they use AI tools in their practice.

Before rolling out AI systems, assess whether staff perceive they will lose autonomy; if so, redesign workflows or training to ensure employees retain meaningful decision-making authority over AI deployment.
AI readiness training alone is insufficient for wellbeing outcomes; organisations must actively protect and communicate about employee agency and control during AI adoption.

articles.title: How AI is reshaping human skills and thinking - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: How AI is reshaping human skills and thinking  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents general psychological perspectives on AI's cognitive impact, but lacks empirical data or multi-country validation. Insights are primarily conceptual rather than evidence-based.
takeaways: Consider how AI tools might atrophy certain cognitive skills (e.g., memory, problem-solving) while amplifying others — design training that preserves critical thinking even as AI handles routine tasks.
Use APA's framing to start conversations with staff about psychological adaptation to AI: how people's sense of competence, autonomy, and professional identity may shift as AI capabilities expand.
Design role redesign interventions that help employees understand *which* skills remain distinctly human (creativity, interpersonal judgment, ethical reasoning) and invest development effort there.

articles.title: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Dual pathways of generative AI use: role ambiguity and self-efficacy in employee-AI collaboration  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample details not evident from title/snippet alone. The psychological constructs (role ambiguity, self-efficacy) are universal, but findings may be limited by sector, organisational context, or geographic scope if not explicitly multi-country.
takeaways: Address role ambiguity by clarifying how AI tools complement (not replace) employee responsibilities—uncertainty about one's AI-adjacent role undermines effective collaboration and adoption.
Build employee self-efficacy through targeted training and early wins with AI tools; confidence in one's ability to work alongside AI is a distinct lever separate from reducing role confusion.
Monitor both pathways when rolling out generative AI: tackling ambiguity alone won't drive adoption if employees doubt their capability, and vice versa.

articles.title: When AI works, employees worry: the vigilance cost of AI delegation in hybrid work - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When AI works, employees worry: the vigilance cost of AI delegation in hybrid work  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not detailed in snippet. Findings on vigilance costs in hybrid work may vary by role type, AI system reliability, and organisational context.
takeaways: Delegating tasks to AI in hybrid settings may create unexpected cognitive load through increased monitoring and anxiety — even when AI performs well — requiring managers to actively support employees' psychological safety around AI use.

Consider implementing clear feedback loops and trust-building mechanisms when introducing AI delegation, as employees working remotely may experience heightened concern about AI reliability without immediate social cues to reassure them.
Design AI workflows that minimise unnecessary vigilance by setting transparent expectations about when and how employees should monitor AI outputs, rather than assuming delegation reduces workload.

articles.title: Transforming work or eroding social capital? How reliance on artificial intelligence drives workplace involution - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Transforming work or eroding social capital? How reliance on artificial intelligence drives workplace involution  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — geographic scope and sample characteristics not evident. Generalisability depends on study design and participant demographics, which cannot be assessed from title and snippet.
takeaways: Monitor whether increased AI adoption in your team is reducing face-to-face collaboration and relationship-building; consider intentional practices to maintain social connection alongside automation.

Be alert to 'workplace involution' — where AI tools create busywork or redundant processes rather than genuine productivity gains; regularly audit whether AI implementations are streamlining or complicating workflows.
Assess trade-offs between efficiency gains from AI and potential erosion of informal knowledge-sharing and mentorship that depend on personal interaction.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner insights are broadly applicable across sectors, but specific case examples and organisational contexts are not detailed in the snippet.
takeaways: Shift framing from 'AI adoption' (one-time implementation) to 'AI adaptation' (ongoing behavioural change) to build sustained capability in your teams.
Design change interventions that target human behaviour and mindset alongside technical rollout, rather than treating culture as a secondary concern.
Identify and address the specific behavioural barriers your organisation faces when integrating AI — this likely requires diagnostic work before designing your change approach.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - nature.com
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design (not clear from title/snippet); likely limited by sector, sample size, and whether findings hold across different organisational contexts and employee demographics.
takeaways: AI awareness can trigger two distinct behavioural pathways in employees: one driven by stress appraisal (threat vs. challenge) and another through job demands-resources theory—understanding which pathway dominates in your workforce helps tailor interventions to support positive job crafting.

Cognitive appraisal matters: employees who appraise AI as a challenge rather than a threat are more likely to proactively reshape their roles; consider how you frame AI introduction and provide psychological safety to shift threat appraisals toward challenge ones.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical research scope. Findings may reflect US business school viewpoint and may not generalise to Australian workplace contexts or non-English speaking regions.
takeaways: Identify specific roles and tasks in your organisation where AI is most likely to create disruption, then design targeted upskilling programmes for those employee groups before changes occur.

Use Stanford's framework to audit your current change management approach — determine whether you're addressing both technical AI skills and the behavioural/psychological adaptation employees need when work processes change.
Engage employees early in AI implementation discussions to surface concerns and co-design adoption strategies, rather than treating AI introduction as a top-down mandate.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's client work and industry observations, but specific case examples and sector focus not detailed in snippet. Findings likely reflect large enterprises and may not transfer directly to smaller organisations or non-profit sectors.
takeaways: Map your AI transformation across three distinct phases (adoption, scaling, impact) to set realistic timelines and resource allocation — moving from pilot projects to embedded, enterprise-wide AI capability requires fundamentally different change management approaches at each horizon.

Identify which business functions or workflows are in each horizon right now, and ensure your workforce development strategy matches the horizon — early-stage adopters need different upskilling than teams optimising AI at scale or measuring business impact.

Use the three-horizon framework to communicate progress to stakeholders and staff — it clarifies why initial AI pilots may show limited ROI, and helps explain what sustained investment and behaviour change are required to move from adoption to genuine organisational impact.

articles.title: Artificial intelligence and media labour transformation in Arab journalism: professional identity, behavioural change, and ethical challenges - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Artificial intelligence and media labour transformation in Arab journalism: professional identity, behavioural change, and ethical challenges  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings are specific to Arab journalism contexts and may not generalise to other regions or non-media sectors. Professional identity and ethical challenges in journalism are sector-specific.
takeaways: Professional identity shifts when AI is introduced; supporting journalists through this transition requires explicit conversation about evolving roles rather than assuming technical training alone drives adoption.

Ethical challenges (bias, accountability, job displacement) emerge as key barriers to behavioural change — address these concerns head-on in change management rather than focusing solely on AI capability building.

Cultural and regional differences in journalism norms and values shape how AI adoption unfolds; one-size-fits-all AI training programmes will miss critical contextual factors that influence acceptance and behaviour change.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG perspective based on consulting experience, likely drawing on global client work, but specific methodologies, sample sizes, and geographic distribution not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability issue first, not just a technology deployment — this shifts focus from tools to the people using them, making behaviour change central to transformation success.

Design change management strategies that address workforce readiness alongside AI implementation; organisations treating these as separate initiatives are more likely to experience adoption resistance and capability gaps.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — likely based on a single study with undisclosed sample characteristics, geographic scope, and methodology.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissism (dominance-seeking, callousness) paradoxically attracts romantic partners in the short term, suggesting personality traits we typically view as 'toxic' can have unexpected social payoffs.

The finding challenges the assumption that narcissistic traits are universally unattractive, hinting at a mismatch between what people say they want in partners and what actually influences attraction.

This reveals a quirk of human psychology: we're drawn to traits signalling confidence and dominance even when those same traits are associated with relationship dysfunction and poor treatment of others.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample size and composition, which are not detailed in the snippet provided. The finding likely applies broadly to how personality shapes memory, though specific limitations cannot be assessed without full methodology.
takeaways: Some personality types remember surprising moments better than others — your personality isn't just about how you behave, it's also about what sticks in your brain.
This challenges the idea that 'surprise' affects everyone's memory equally; individual differences matter more than we typically assume when something unexpected happens.
A neat reminder that the same shocking event gets encoded and recalled differently depending on who you are — fascinating for understanding why people's accounts of the same surprise diverge so much.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline-style news summary without methodology details, likely reporting on a single neuroimaging study with unclear sample characteristics and geographic scope.
takeaways: Brain structure and function genuinely do differ between people with psychopathic traits and others — it's not just behavioral performance or choice.
Neuroimaging findings about personality differences feel surprising because we tend to think of psychology as separate from biology, but the brain quite literally is the source of personality.
These kinds of studies raise the philosophical puzzle: if psychopathy has a neural basis, how much responsibility can we assign to individuals for traits rooted in brain architecture?

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings depend on the specific AI model used, the dataset of wine reviews analysed, and whether patterns hold across different languages, regions, or wine-tasting cultures.
takeaways: Wine review language appears to reveal personality traits — what people choose to focus on (flavour complexity vs. price value, emotional impressions vs. technical details) may signal whether they're conscientious, open-minded, or pragmatic.
AI can spot personality signals in everyday writing that humans might miss, suggesting our casual preferences and how we describe them leak clues about who we are.
The finding is fun because it flips the script — you might think wine reviews are just about the wine, but they're accidentally broadcasting your personality to anyone (or anything) paying attention.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Findings suggest cross-cultural patterns in how personality traits correlate with music taste, though sample composition and methodology not detailed in snippet.
takeaways: People's music preferences reveal consistent personality patterns worldwide — suggesting that 'taste in music' might be a universal window into how someone thinks and behaves.

The link between personality and music preference appears strong enough to transcend cultural boundaries, making it one of the more reliably predictive personality markers across different populations.

This challenges the idea that music taste is purely learned or culturally determined — there may be something fundamental about personality that gravitates toward certain musical characteristics regardless of where you grow up.

articles.title: A new era of weight loss: Mental health effects of GLP-1 drugs - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: A new era of weight loss: Mental health effects of GLP-1 drugs  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on US context and American Psychological Association perspective. Mental health effects may vary by individual, dosage, and concurrent treatment, so findings should not be generalised universally.
takeaways: GLP-1 drugs (like semaglutide) are showing unexpected psychological side effects alongside weight loss — a reminder that biological interventions can have complex mental health ripple effects that aren't always obvious upfront.

The intersection of rapid physical change and mental wellbeing is more intricate than simple cause-and-effect — people losing weight quickly may experience mood shifts, identity changes, or relationship impacts that deserve clinical attention.

This highlights why psychological assessment should accompany pharmacological weight-loss interventions, not follow them — the mental health conversation needs to happen before and during treatment, not as an afterthought.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geography not specified in snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings are specific to academic settings and multicultural team contexts. The generalisability to corporate or other organisational sectors is unclear. Geographic scope and sample size cannot be determined from the snippet provided.
takeaways: AI tools may help leaders identify and mitigate unconscious gender bias in multicultural teams, but their effectiveness depends on how leadership uses the insights — ensure AI recommendations are paired with genuine commitment to inclusive decision-making.

Monitor whether AI-assisted inclusion becomes performative (checking a box) rather than transformative; focus on measurable changes in gendered outcomes like speaking time, project assignments, and advancement opportunities within your team.
Consider piloting AI-assisted feedback or decision support in high-stakes moments (hiring, promotion, project allocation) where gender and cultural bias is most likely to distort outcomes.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - nature.com
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  nature.com
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The mechanisms identified (psychological safety and ethical leadership as mediators between AI adoption and depression) are likely applicable across sectors, but geographic scope, sample size, and industry composition require examination of the full paper.
takeaways: AI adoption can negatively impact employee wellbeing through reduced psychological safety — leaders must actively maintain trust and safe-to-speak environments during AI implementation, not assume adoption proceeds without social cost.

Ethical leadership is protective: organisations that combine AI adoption with transparent communication about AI's role, clear ethical guardrails, and leader accountability for fair implementation can mitigate depression and disengagement in their workforce.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's insights are based on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample size, methodology, and geographic scope are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Create explicit norms that invite and reward speaking up without fear of embarrassment or retaliation, particularly for employees from underrepresented groups who may perceive higher social risk.

Assess whether your current team dynamics inadvertently create unequal psychological safety — some voices may feel safer to speak than others depending on hierarchy, identity, or prior experience of being heard.

Use psychological safety initiatives to surface diverse perspectives and challenge assumptions, which directly improves decision-making and innovation rather than treating it as a standalone 'nice-to-have'.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: Moderate — PwC's global workforce survey typically covers multiple countries and sectors, but sample composition, response rates, and demographic representation are not specified in the snippet, which limits assessment of how findings generalise across different organisational contexts and geographies.
takeaways: Use survey data on workforce anxieties to diagnose psychological safety gaps in your organisation — compare findings against your own employee feedback to identify which fears (e.g. job security, AI impact, career progression) are most acute in your teams.

Frame psychological safety interventions around the specific hopes and fears identified in the survey data relevant to your sector — this evidence base can help leadership understand that addressing these concerns is not 'nice-to-have' but linked to retention and engagement.

Monitor whether your organisation's communication and policies are inadvertently amplifying fears (e.g. around automation) — use the survey as a conversation starter with managers to co-design reassurance strategies grounded in what employees actually worry about.

articles.title: Reframing workplace safety, wellbeing, and performance among operating room nurses in contemporary healthcare systems - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Reframing workplace safety, wellbeing, and performance among operating room nurses in contemporary healthcare systems  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited to operating room nursing context; findings may not generalise to other healthcare settings or non-healthcare sectors without further validation. Geographic scope unclear from snippet.
takeaways: Psychological safety in high-stakes clinical environments requires explicit reframing of how safety concerns are communicated and escalated — OR nurses need structured channels to raise near-misses without fear of blame.
Linking psychological safety directly to patient outcomes and team performance (not just individual wellbeing) can motivate leadership buy-in for safety-first cultures in healthcare teams.

Operating room settings demand integration of safety, wellbeing, and performance as interconnected outcomes; siloed approaches to any one factor risk undermining the others in time-critical situations.

articles.title: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams - Deloitte
articles.snippet: Human capabilities are at the heart of high-performing teams  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Limited — typical of Deloitte consulting reports, likely drawn from client work and industry observations rather than rigorous research. Findings may reflect practices among large organisations that engage Deloitte, with unclear generalisability to small-to-medium enterprises or non-client sectors.
takeaways: Psychological safety depends on deliberate cultivation of human capabilities (trust, communication, vulnerability) rather than structural fixes alone — assess whether your team development programs prioritise interpersonal skill-building alongside technical training.

High-performing teams require leaders to model and reinforce psychological safety through demonstrated competence and authenticity; audit your own leadership behaviours and those of managers for consistency between stated values and actions.

Identify specific capability gaps in your team (e.g. active listening, conflict resolution, giving/receiving feedback) and design targeted interventions rather than generic team-building, since generic activities rarely move the psychological safety needle.
